cards.title: GNPS Program 8: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series · Mental Health Nursing

cards.title: Welcome to Program 8
cards.body: Mental health nursing is grounded in respect, empathy, safety and partnership. Nurses encounter people experiencing emotional distress, mental illness, substance-related problems and behavioural change across every healthcare setting — not only specialist services.

bullets.label: This programme is designed around the mental
bullets.text: This programme is designed around the mental health capabilities expected by nursing regulatory bodies worldwide, developing the knowledge, assessment skills and professional behaviours required for person-centred, recovery-oriented care.

bullets.label: Explain mental health, mental illness and recovery-oriented practice
Build a therapeutic nurse-person relationship using empathy and trust
Conduct a basic mental health assessment and mental state examination
Identify risk of self-harm, suicide, aggression and clinical deterioration
Understand common psychotropic medicines and monitoring needs

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: Compassionate. Recovery-Oriented. Safe.

bullets.label: By the end of Level 1, you will be able to
bullets.text: By the end of Level 1, you will be able to provide compassionate, recovery-oriented mental health nursing care, complete a person-centred assessment and respond safely to common mental health risks within your scope of practice.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing

bullets.label: Mental health nursing recognises the person
bullets.text: Mental health nursing recognises the person beyond the diagnosis. Recovery does not always mean the complete absence of symptoms — it may mean living a meaningful, hopeful and self-directed life while managing ongoing challenges.

bullets.label: Nurses support recovery by listening, respecting choice, identifying strengths and actively reducing stigma.

cards.title: Core Concepts: Foundations
cards.body: Mental Health Continuum

bullets.label: Influenced by biological, psychological,
bullets.text: Influenced by biological, psychological, social, cultural and environmental factors. Distress can exist without a formal diagnosis.

bullets.label: Supports hope, choice, identity, meaning and
bullets.text: Supports hope, choice, identity, meaning and participation. The person is an active partner, not a passive recipient of care.

bullets.label: Stigma affects employment, housing and
bullets.text: Stigma affects employment, housing and healthcare access. Nurses challenge stigmatising language and attitudes every day.

bullets.label: Mental and physical health are interconnected.
bullets.text: Mental and physical health are interconnected. Sleep, nutrition, trauma, relationships and social conditions all require consideration.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Mr Khan
cards.body: "I am more than this illness."

bullets.label: The nurse asks about his goals, strengths and
bullets.text: The nurse asks about his goals, strengths and what has helped previously. Together they identify sleep, social contact and return to study as important recovery goals alongside treatment.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Therapeutic Communication & Professional Relationships

bullets.label: The therapeutic relationship is purposeful,
bullets.text: The therapeutic relationship is purposeful, time-limited and focused on the person's needs. Trust develops through consistency, empathy, honesty and clear professional boundaries.

cards.title: Therapeutic vs. Non-Therapeutic Responses
cards.body: ✅ Therapeutic Responses

bullets.label: Overwhelming questions when trust is low
"It sounds as though things feel hopeless right now. Can you tell me more about what has been happening?"
— Example of a validating, therapeutic response

cards.title: Professional Boundaries in Mental Health Nursing
cards.body: Boundaries protect both the person and the nurse. They are a cornerstone of safe, ethical practice.

bullets.label: All care decisions should be transparent and documented
Personal financial relationships are never appropriate
Keep focus on the person's needs, not your own

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Mental Health Assessment & Common Conditions

bullets.label: A mental health assessment combines the
bullets.text: A mental health assessment combines the person's story, observed behaviour, mental state, physical health and current risks. It should be collaborative — never reduced to a checklist.

bullets.label: Each component informs the others — assessment is a dynamic, ongoing conversation, not a one-time event.

cards.title: Recognising Common Mental Health Conditions
cards.body: Mood Disorders

bullets.label: Depression: low mood, loss of interest, sleep
bullets.text: Depression: low mood, loss of interest, sleep and appetite changes, hopelessness. Mania: elevated mood, reduced sleep, rapid speech, risky behaviour.

bullets.label: Ranges from persistent worry and social anxiety
bullets.text: Ranges from persistent worry and social anxiety to acute panic attacks. Physical symptoms often accompany psychological distress.

bullets.label: May involve hallucinations, delusions and
bullets.text: May involve hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thought. Assess meaning, impact and safety — never argue about beliefs.

bullets.label: Intoxication, withdrawal, delirium and dementia
bullets.text: Intoxication, withdrawal, delirium and dementia require careful distinction, especially in older adults. Assess thoroughly before concluding.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Hearing Voices
cards.body: A patient reports hearing a voice telling him to harm himself.

bullets.label: Does he intend to act on it?
What access does he have to means?
What helps him resist the voice?
The response remains calm, respectful and focused on safety throughout.
Direct questions do not create suicidal ideas
Plan, access and timeline all matter
What keeps the person safe right now?

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Crisis, Safety & Psychotropic Medication

bullets.label: Mental health crises may involve suicidal
bullets.text: Mental health crises may involve suicidal thoughts, self-harm, aggression, severe withdrawal, panic, mania or psychosis. The nurse must protect safety while preserving dignity, always choosing the least restrictive effective response.

cards.title: De-escalation & Psychotropic Medicine Safety
cards.body: De-escalation Principles

bullets.label: Reduce noise, maintain respectful space, offer clear choices
Restraint or seclusion only when required by law and policy
Call for help before a situation escalates further
Narrow therapeutic window — monitor levels closely
Anxiolytics and antipsychotics — monitor airway and consciousness

cards.title: End of Program Summary
cards.body: Ready for What Comes Next

bullets.label: By completing GNPS Program 8 — Level 1, you
bullets.text: By completing GNPS Program 8 — Level 1, you have developed foundational knowledge and practical skills in recovery-oriented care, therapeutic communication, mental health assessment and crisis safety response.

bullets.label: These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 —
bullets.text: These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex risk, law, medication management and multidisciplinary practice.

cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8 · Level 1 – Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Section 1: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
cards.body: What Is Recovery?

bullets.label: Recovery does not always mean the complete
bullets.text: Recovery does not always mean the complete absence of symptoms. It means living a meaningful, hopeful and self-directed life while managing ongoing challenges.

bullets.label: Mental health nurses recognise the whole person beyond diagnosis. They support recovery by:

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Explain mental health, mental illness and wellbeing
Articulate the principles of recovery-oriented practice
Recognise biological, social and cultural factors affecting mental health

cards.title: Mental Health & Wellbeing
cards.body: Mental health exists on a continuum — influenced by biological, psychological, social, cultural and environmental factors.

bullets.label: A person may experience significant distress without meeting diagnostic criteria for a disorder.
Another person may live a fulfilling life while managing a long-term mental health condition.
Mental health fluctuates over time and responds to circumstances, relationships and support.

cards.title: Recovery-Oriented Practice
cards.body: Core Principles

bullets.label: Recovery-oriented care positions the person as an active partner — not a passive recipient of treatment.
Believing a meaningful life is possible
Seeing the person beyond their diagnosis
Supporting inclusion in community and social life

cards.title: Stigma & Discrimination
cards.body: Why It Matters

bullets.label: Stigma creates real barriers for people living with mental health conditions. It can impact:
Nurses actively challenge stigmatising language
bullets.text: Nurses actively challenge stigmatising language and attitudes — in clinical conversations, documentation and team discussions.

cards.title: Holistic Mental Health Care
cards.body: Mental and physical health are deeply interconnected. Effective care considers the whole person.

bullets.label: Fundamental to mood regulation and cognitive function
Unresolved trauma and chronic pain affect mental wellbeing
Review for interactions, side effects and substance use
Social conditions, culture and connection shape recovery

cards.title: Clinical Example: Mr Khan
cards.body: "I am more than this illness."

bullets.label: Mr Khan lives with recurrent depression. Rather
bullets.text: Mr Khan lives with recurrent depression. Rather than focusing only on symptoms, his nurse takes a strengths-based approach.

bullets.label: Improving sleep as a priority goal
Return to study as a meaningful aspiration
The nurse's approach illustrates
bullets.text: The nurse's approach illustrates recovery-oriented practice — listening, collaborating and building on the person's own vision for their life.

cards.title: Factors Influencing Mental Health
cards.body: Mental health is shaped by a complex interplay of factors. Nurses assess across all dimensions to provide truly person-centred care.

bullets.label: Coping styles, trauma history, self-esteem, cognition
Housing, employment, income, access to services

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: 👁 See the Person

bullets.label: Look beyond the diagnosis to the individual's strengths, goals and identity
Foster self-determination and belief that a meaningful life is achievable
Model respectful language and attitudes in every clinical interaction
Include physical, social, cultural and environmental needs in every assessment
NCLEX Connection: Recovery-oriented principles
bullets.text: NCLEX Connection: Recovery-oriented principles underpin questions on psychosocial integrity — expect scenarios testing therapeutic communication, patient autonomy and holistic assessment.

cards.title: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8: Compassionate Mental Health Care

cards.title: Why the Therapeutic Relationship Matters
cards.body: The therapeutic relationship is the cornerstone of mental health nursing. Unlike social relationships, it is:

bullets.label: Focused on the person's recovery and wellbeing
Built through consistency, empathy, honesty and clear boundaries

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: Use attentive, empathic listening in clinical encounters
Recognise and avoid responses that close down discussion
Maintain safe, respectful limits that protect both nurse and patient

cards.title: Active Listening: More Than Just Hearing
cards.body: Active listening is a deliberate, skilled practice that communicates respect and creates space for the person to organise their thoughts and feelings.

bullets.label: Open body language, appropriate eye contact
Allowing space without rushing to fill it
Mirroring the person's words back to them
Drawing together key themes at the right moment

cards.title: Therapeutic vs. Non-Therapeutic Responses
cards.body: The way a nurse responds can open or close a therapeutic conversation. Therapeutic responses invite the person to share more; non-therapeutic responses can inadvertently shut down disclosure.

bullets.label: Avoid saying "You'll be fine" — it dismisses the person's experience rather than validating it.

cards.title: Clinical Focus
cards.body: Responding to Distress

bullets.label: When a person is anxious, withdrawn or suspicious…
One question at a time, with patience
Consistency over time is more powerful than any single interaction

cards.title: Professional Boundaries in Practice
cards.body: Boundaries protect both the person and the nurse, preserving the integrity of the therapeutic relationship. Boundary violations — even unintentional ones — can cause lasting harm.

bullets.label: Do not keep information hidden from the care team
Never accept gifts or engage in financial transactions
Share only what directly benefits the patient's care
The relationship must stay within the therapeutic role

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Putting It All Together

bullets.label: This dismisses the person's distress and shuts down further communication.
"It sounds as though things feel hopeless right now. Can you tell me more about what has been happening?"
This validates distress, demonstrates empathy and opens further assessment.
The therapeutic response validates the feeling,
bullets.text: The therapeutic response validates the feeling, avoids false reassurance, and invites the person to share — all in one sentence.

cards.title: The Communication Process: Step by Step
cards.body: Adapt & Respond

bullets.label: Effective mental health communication is not a
bullets.text: Effective mental health communication is not a script — it is a responsive, cyclical process that the nurse adapts in real time based on the person's cues, state and needs.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Section 2 Summary

bullets.label: Always listen before offering solutions or advice
Validate feelings rather than minimising them with false comfort
Tailor communication to the person's current mental state
Clear, respectful limits protect everyone in the therapeutic relationship

cards.title: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8 · Level 1 Qualified Nurse

cards.title: What Is a Mental Health Assessment?
cards.body: A mental health assessment combines the person's story, observed behaviour, mental state, physical health and current risks into a holistic picture.

bullets.label: The assessment should be collaborative — it must never reduce a person to a checklist.
Consider physical and psychological factors together

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Perform a structured mental state examination with confidence.
Evaluate mood, thought, perception and cognition systematically.
Identify common mental health presentations accurately.
Identify changes that require escalation or further assessment.

cards.title: The Mental State Examination (MSE)
cards.body: The MSE provides a structured framework to describe a patient's psychological functioning at a point in time.

bullets.label: Dress, hygiene, eye contact, psychomotor activity
Rate, tone, volume; subjective emotional state
Observed emotional expression; form and content of thinking
Orientation, memory, concentration; awareness of illness

cards.title: Mood and Anxiety Disorders
cards.body: Key Assessment Points

bullets.label: Mood disorders span a wide spectrum. Accurate assessment guides safe and effective care planning.
Depression: Low mood, anhedonia, appetite and sleep disturbance, hopelessness
Mania: Elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, impulsive behaviour
Anxiety: Persistent worry, physical symptoms, panic episodes
Always assess for suicidal ideation when screening for depression.

cards.title: Psychotic Disorders
cards.body: Psychosis disrupts a person's perception of reality and requires careful, non-confrontational assessment.

bullets.label: Perceptions without external stimulus —
bullets.text: Perceptions without external stimulus — auditory, visual or tactile. Ask directly: "Are you hearing things others cannot hear?"

bullets.label: Fixed false beliefs resistant to reasoning.
bullets.text: Fixed false beliefs resistant to reasoning. Assess their meaning, impact and safety implications — never argue about the belief.

bullets.label: Loose associations, tangential or incoherent speech. Observe for reduced functioning in daily activities.

cards.title: Substance Use and Cognitive Change
cards.body: Overlapping Presentations

bullets.label: Substance use, delirium, dementia and
bullets.text: Substance use, delirium, dementia and depression can all alter behaviour and cognition — careful differentiation is essential, especially in older adults.

bullets.label: Intoxication/Withdrawal: Acute behavioural change and elevated risk
Delirium: Acute onset, fluctuating consciousness — potentially reversible
Dementia: Gradual cognitive decline affecting memory and function

cards.title: CLINICAL EXAMPLE
cards.body: Assessing a Patient Reporting Auditory Hallucinations

bullets.label: "A patient reports hearing a voice telling him to harm himself."
The nurse responds calmly and asks a structured set of safety-focused questions.
"Do you feel like acting on what it tells you?"
"Do you have access to anything you could use to harm yourself?"
The nurse's response is calm, respectful and focused on safety throughout the interaction.

cards.title: Assessment Best Practice
cards.body: Person-centred

bullets.label: Differentiate Carefully - separate psychiatric symptoms from delirium or intoxication
Document Objectively - record clear, unbiased findings
Ask Directly - inquire about hallucinations and suicidal thoughts
Observe & Converse - combine observation with conversation
Following these principles ensures assessments
bullets.text: Following these principles ensures assessments are thorough, person-centred and clinically sound — reducing risk and supporting recovery.

cards.title: Section 3 — Key Takeaways
cards.body: Observe & Engage

bullets.label: Combine structured observation with therapeutic conversation.
Do not avoid asking about hallucinations, self-harm or suicide.
Distinguish psychiatric illness from delirium, dementia or substance effects.
Record findings objectively to support the wider clinical team.

decks.title: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 8 - Level 1 - Section 4 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
cards.body: GNPS Programme 8 · Mental Health Nursing · Section 4

bullets.label: Supporting recovery through safe, compassionate, and least restrictive care.

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series
cards.body: What You Will Learn

bullets.label: By the end of this section, you will be
bullets.text: By the end of this section, you will be equipped to respond safely and compassionately to mental health crises in clinical practice.

bullets.label: Recognise immediate mental health risks including suicidal ideation and aggression.
Apply de-escalation strategies using least restrictive, dignity-preserving approaches.
Respond appropriately to suicidal behaviour, self-harm, and aggression.
Recognise serious psychotropic medication risks and adverse reactions.

cards.title: Understanding Mental Health Crises
cards.body: Mental health crises can present as suicidal thoughts, self-harm, aggression, severe withdrawal, panic, mania, or psychosis. The nurse's priority is to protect safety while preserving the patient's dignity — always choosing the least restrictive effective response.

bullets.label: The nurse's role is not to judge, but to assess, respond, and advocate.

cards.title: Suicide and Self-Harm Risk Assessment
cards.body: Key Assessment Areas

bullets.label: Direct, compassionate questioning does not plant suicidal ideas. It is both safe and necessary.
Thoughts: Is the patient thinking about suicide or self-harm?
Plan and intent: Do they have a specific plan?
Means: Do they have access to those means?
Protective factors: Family, hope, reason to live
When risk is high, immediate safety planning and escalation are required.

cards.title: De-escalation in Practice
cards.body: Early, calm intervention can prevent a crisis from escalating. The nurse's presence, tone, and environment all matter.

bullets.label: Use a steady, respectful tone. Avoid raised voices or confrontational language.
Maintain a safe, non-threatening physical distance. Avoid blocking exits.
Give the patient a sense of control by offering simple, realistic options.
Lower noise, limit bystanders, and create a calmer environment when possible.

cards.title: Least Restrictive Practice
cards.body: Restriction, restraint, or seclusion must only be used in accordance with law and policy, and only when less restrictive measures are insufficient to manage a serious, immediate risk.

bullets.label: Reduce triggers, offer space, minimise stimulation

cards.title: Psychotropic Medications: Key Risks
cards.body: Nurses must monitor patients on psychotropic medications closely. Serious reactions can be life-threatening and require prompt recognition and escalation.

bullets.label: Agitation, tremor, hyperthermia — linked to antidepressants
Nausea, tremor, confusion — requires urgent blood levels
Rigidity, fever, altered consciousness — antipsychotic emergency
Seizures, delirium — especially with anxiolytics and alcohol

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Putting It All Together

bullets.label: Pacing and shouting observed. Nurse notes early warning signs.
Nurse reduces noise, removes bystanders, creates calm space.
Calm tone, respectful distance, clear choices offered. Support called early.
Patient states intent to attack another person — team activates emergency protocol immediately.

cards.title: NCLEX Focus: What You Must Know
cards.body: These core principles are frequently tested in NCLEX and competency assessments for internationally qualified nurses.

bullets.label: Always ask directly about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, and means. It does not increase risk.
Use de-escalation as a first-line response before any restrictive intervention.
Restraint or seclusion is a last resort — legal, time-limited, and always documented.
Know the serious adverse effects of antidepressants, mood stabilisers, antipsychotics, and anxiolytics.

cards.title: Section 4 Complete
cards.body: "Support recovery. Promote wellbeing."

bullets.label: You have completed Section 4: Crisis, Safety
bullets.text: You have completed Section 4: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication. You are now prepared to identify mental health risks, apply de-escalation safely, and monitor psychotropic medications with confidence.

bullets.label: Review your understanding of crisis response and medication safety
Apply these principles through case studies and simulation
